desc: https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ex2606-dive10-biology-HD.mp4 While marine life seen during the tenth dive of the 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping Exploration expedition wasn’t plentiful, it was present. From amphipods clinging to a dead sponge stalk to sea cucumbers, polychaete worms, and a benthic ctenophore with incredibly long (meters long) feeding tentacles, the dive reinforced that even with the harsh temperatures, pressures, and other conditions found at depths over 5,500 meters (3.4 miles), life still finds a way to thrive at the bottom of the ocean.

desc: https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ex2606-dive10-nodules_HD.mp4 During Dive 10 of the 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping Exploration expedition, the team observed very large polymetallic nodules, some as large as 10 centimeters (4 inches) or greater in diameter. Nodules form around hard materials, such as fossilized shark teeth or fragments of rock, slowly accumulating around this nucleus. The large size of the nodules seen during the dive suggest that they may have been growing for a very long time. Video courtesy of NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping Exploration.

title: EX2605 Dive 06 Nodule Field
caption: During Dive 06 of the 2026 Cook Islands ROV Exploration cruise, we encountered a field of dense polymetallic nodules of various sizes and shapes on the seafloor. These nodules form over millions of years, as sediment and minerals accumulate around a hard nucleus made of something like a sediment clump or a shark tooth.

desc: https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/ex2606-dive12-sponge_HD.mp4 During Dive 12 of the 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping Exploration expedition, the team encountered this sponge, Caulophacus oxydiscus, that towered an impressive +3 meters tall (9.8 feet) with a head that was 50 centimeters (20 inches) across. The sponge was growing almost perpendicular to the seafloor, rising into the water column to gain better access to food floating by. Video courtesy of NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping Exploration.

title: Anemone
caption: An anemone (Relicanthus daphneae) with its tentacles flowing in the current. This individual was seen in a crack on a sheer rock face on Kaʻena Slope during Dive 08 of the 2025 ROV and Mapping Shakedown expedition. Dive 08 was one of two dives focused on testing a new lighting system with the cameras on remotely operated vehicle Deep Discoverer. Video courtesy of NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2025 Beyond the Blue.

title: Halosaur
caption: This halosaur was seen swimming just above the seafloor at a depth of 5,510 meters during Dive 09 of the 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping Exploration expedition. Image courtesy of NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping Exploration. Download largest version (jpg, 512 KB).

title: Deep-Sea Squid (Magnapinna sp.)
caption: This very rare deep-sea squid (Magnapinna sp.) was among the more than 400 different species seen in the deep waters of the Cook Islands, the vast majority of which were recorded there for the first time. Other animals included sponges, corals, anemones, crustaceans, gastropods, fish, urchins, and other cephalopods.

title: Urchin
caption: A white urchin makes its way across the heavily sedimented seafloor explored during the eleventh dive of the 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping Exploration expedition. Image courtesy of NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping Exploration. Download largest version (jpg, 808 KB).

title: Polymetallic Nodules
caption: Polymetallic nodules covered the seafloor explored during the tenth dive of the 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping Exploration expedition. We saw the highest abundance of nodules during this dive out of any dive on the expedition thus far. Image courtesy of NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping Exploration. Download largest version (jpg, 905 KB).

title: Nodule Field
caption: Throughout Dive 09 of the 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping Exploration expedition, we observed a relatively homogenous distribution of polymetallic nodules covering less than 50% of the seafloor. Image courtesy of NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping Exploration. Download largest version (jpg, 826 KB).

title: Swimming Sea Cucumber
caption: Yellow swimming sea cucumber (Enypniastes eximia) covered in hydroids seen just before the remotely operated vehicles reached the seafloor on the Kaʻena Slope during Dive 08 of the 2025 ROV and Mapping Shakedown expedition.

title: Deep Discoverer
caption: Remotely operated vehicle Deep Discoverer on deck of NOAA Ship Okeanos Explorer following a dunk test while in port during the 2026 ROV Shakedown expedition. Image courtesy of NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2026 ROV Shakedown.

title: ROV Deep Discoverer
caption: Top-down view of remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Deep Discoverer, captured from ROV Seirios during Dive 11 of the 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping Exploration expedition. Seirios is tethered via a cable to NOAA Ship Okeanos Explorer and Deep Discoverer, absorbing ship heave to keep Deep Discoverer stable while providing power, data transfer, and an expanded view for ROV pilots. Image courtesy of NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping Exploration. Download largest version (jpg, 194 KB).

title: ROV Seirios
caption: A top-down view of remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Deep Discoverer exploring the seafloor. Captured from ROV Seirios during Dive 13 of the 2026 Cook Islands ROV Exploration cruise.

title: ROV Deep Discoverer
caption: Remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) Deep Discoverer — seen here during the 2026 ROV Shakedown — and Seirios are owned by NOAA Ocean Exploration and maintained and operated by the NOAA Ocean Exploration Cooperative Institute. Capable of diving to depths of 6,000 meters (3.7 miles), the pair provide scientists invaluable access to the deep ocean. With Deep Discoverer, we’re able to capture high-definition video, collect biological, geological, and water samples, and measure physical characteristics of the ocean such as salinity, water temperature, depth, and dissolved oxygen to help us better understand the deep-ocean environment. Image courtesy of NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2026 ROV Shakedown. Download largest version (jpg, 2.56 MB).
